seo.title: Karmic tail 18 18 18 compatibility: three Moons of a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 18 18 compatibility: three Moons and The Hermit at the centre — what the tail means for a couple and why its story is a truth seen in a mirror.

title: The 18-18-18 tail in compatibility: three Moons and a truth seen in a mirror
short: The Moon, The Moon and The Moon again: the 18-18-18 tail holds no other card, and it turns up in roughly one couple in 1,684. In compatibility this karmic tail means that two people come together over a mystery, live their union in half-light, where each sees the other by reflected light, and are handed a single main task — to stop knowing each other by reflection.

sections.h2: The novel where the key evidence was seen in a mirror
paragraphs: In 1868 Wilkie Collins published The Moonstone, a novel T. S. Eliot would later call "the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels". At its centre is a yellow diamond. Legend says it was set in the forehead of an Indian god of the Moon, its lustre "growing and lessening … with the waxing and waning of the moon"; hence the stone's name. A will leaves the diamond to Rachel Verinder as a present for her eighteenth birthday, 21 June 1848. The Moon is the eighteenth arcanum too. Collins knew nothing of the destiny matrix, and a coincidence stays a coincidence, but it is an easy one to remember.

That same night the stone vanishes. Suspicion falls on a housemaid with a dark past, on Indian jugglers prowling round the house, and finally on Rachel herself: the celebrated Sergeant Cuff seriously concludes that she has stolen her own diamond. Yet Rachel knows from the first minute who the thief is. She saw him. It is Franklin Blake, her cousin and the man she loves.

She did not see him directly. He stood with his back to her at the Indian cabinet, and Rachel watched in a mirror: "There are three glasses in my sitting-room. As you stood there, I saw all that you did, reflected in one of them." Three mirrors in the room, three Moons in the tail. The key evidence in this love story is a reflection, and a true one: the hand really did take the stone from the drawer. Everything else was wrong. Franklin remembered nothing: he had been secretly dosed with laudanum, and that night he walked as if in a dream.

Collins said himself what the book stands on. In the preface of 1868: "The conduct pursued, under a sudden emergency, by a young girl, supplies the foundation on which I have built this book." That conduct is silence. Rachel saw, and said not a word — not to her mother, not to the police, not to him. The plot of the novel stands on that silence, and so does the plot of a couple with three Moons. Quotations from the novel here and below are Collins's own words.

sections.h2: The first Moon, entry to the task: a door painted by two
paragraphs: Entry to the task is the first card of the couple's tail. For Lisovskaya it is what two people want together, their agreements and their "common language". The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also turn into resistance. With The Moon at the entry, the couple's common language is mystery.

In the novel that language is visible before the theft. For weeks Rachel and Franklin decorate the door of her little sitting-room with griffins, birds, flowers and cupids, copied from designs by a famous Italian painter. They mix the paint with a "vehicle" Franklin invented himself; it stinks so badly that the very dogs sneeze when they come into the room. The old house-steward Betteredge grumbles but admits that the two never seemed to tire of it, sitting over the door "with their heads together, as busy as bees". They finish on the birthday itself, by three in the afternoon. The pattern is beautiful and so tangled that, Betteredge says, "you felt them unpleasantly in your head for hours after".

And what draws them to each other is what cannot be seen to the end. Of the diamond Betteredge writes that a stone you could hold between finger and thumb "seemed unfathomable as the heavens themselves". Of Rachel he says almost the same: "The difficulty was to fathom Miss Rachel." Franklin, as Betteredge describes him, has "his French side, and his German side, and his Italian side", with the original English foundation only now and then showing through; Rachel teases him about which side is uppermost. Each loves in the other a depth with no bottom.

Now the catch. The vehicle takes twelve hours to dry, and Franklin painted the last morsel of the pattern himself, at about three in the afternoon. At night the paint is still wet, and whoever passed brushed against it. The smear on the door became the first clue. The couple's shared picture keeps a trace of every night. This is the double nature of the entry: the world of images two people create together is their language and, at the same time, the place where their future misunderstanding is written down.

The numbers add their own clue. In this couple the Moon at the entry is always folded from two different cards: one partner has The Devil (15) at this point, the other The Empress (3). Our reading: enchantment plus shared creation. Betteredge confesses that the diamond "laid such a hold on" him that he cried out "O" along with the young ladies; The Empress is the generosity that grows living, beautiful things. Together they make a door covered in cupids.

In life this is recognisable at once. The couple has pet words no third person would understand, an invented world of their own — a city, a game, a series, an unusual shared passion. They like it that even friends understand them only in part. In Lisovskaya, The Moon fills a union with fantasy and play for two, and at the entry that is the glue. Resistance starts with a sentence that sounds like a compliment: "we understand each other without words". From it the next one follows easily: so words need not check anything.

sections.h2: The second Moon, the middle: a year of silence for the other's sake
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from their shared wish to the main task. With The Moon in the middle, that road runs through dusk.

Rachel later describes the birthday night. At about one o'clock she cannot sleep, lights her candle and means to fetch a book from the sitting-room. There is light under the door, footsteps. She thinks it is her mother, who spent the evening begging to take charge of the diamond, and blows out her own candle so as to seem asleep. From the dark she sees Franklin "in your nightgown — with your bedroom candle in your hand". In the mirror she watches him open the drawers, take out the stone and stand still for a long time: "I saw your face sideways in the glass. You looked like a man thinking, and dissatisfied with his own thoughts." Then his light went away, and she was left alone in the dark.

Then comes a year. Rachel raises no alarm. She refuses to have her wardrobe examined, cries out to the police officer that she never sent for him and that nobody will ever find the diamond, cuts off all contact with Franklin and tells no one why. Before morning she writes him a letter that names nothing openly: only a hint that she knows of his debts, and a private offer to lend him money. The letter never reaches him. Franklin sees only that the woman he loves has turned to ice and will not see him. He leaves England.

So two versions of one story appear. In hers he is a thief who also pretends to zeal and hunts for himself. In his she has come to hate him for no reason at all. Among The Moon's tasks for a couple Lisovskaya names jealousy and grievances that most often grow out of invented stories. The novel shows how such stories are born: from a real fact seen only in part.

The hardest thing about the middle is that the silence here is not a lie. Betteredge remembers Rachel as a child: when a friend she loved was at fault, she took the blame, never confessed and never lied. She looked you straight in the face and said plainly, "I won't tell you!" Her mother kept saying: "Rachel's best friend and Rachel's worst enemy are, one and the other — Rachel herself." The grown-up Rachel is silent out of love: "I spare him, when my heart is breaking; I screen him when my own character is at stake." And from outside, a silent person looks guilty — the detective suspected her of all people.

In Paul's hymn to love, charity "beareth all things" (1 Cor 13:7). The Greek verb is στέγει, from στέγη, "roof": to cover, to keep under a roof, to keep silent. Thayer's lexicon notes that some interpreters read the verse exactly so — love covers and hides the faults of others; Thayer himself prefers "beareth", but the Greek word holds both senses. Rachel loved in just that way, by covering. Yet one line earlier the same hymn says that love "rejoiceth in the truth". To cover without knowing the truth — that is the second Moon.

The numbers leave a clue here as well. The middle of this couple's tail is folded from The Hierophant (5) of one partner and Death (13) of the other. Our reading: a rule plus a rupture. "One doesn't talk about such things", "I won't humiliate him with a question" — and instead of a conversation, a door closes. The year of fog is made of a code of honour and a break.

In life it looks ordinary. One partner notices a fragment — an odd pause in a conversation, a phrase half overheard, a closed door — and does not ask, so as not to humiliate either of them. The other feels the chill and does not ask either, so as not to seem clingy. Each protects the other with silence and runs a private investigation. Nobody lies, and both are wrong.

All this time the key evidence lay at the bottom. Franklin's nightgown with the smear of paint was found by a housemaid secretly in love with him, who hid it in a tin case in the Shivering Sand by the sea. Of that quicksand Betteredge writes that at the turn of the tide "something goes on in the unknown deeps below", and the whole surface begins to tremble. A truth hidden out of love lies down there and shudders with every tide. That is how the second Moon feels: nothing has been said aloud, yet everything keeps shaking.

sections.h2: The third Moon, the main task: "I saw you with my own eyes"
paragraphs: The main task is the anchor point of the tail. Lisovskaya reads it mostly through its minus: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn.

A year later Franklin finds the case in the sand, unrolls the nightgown and looks for the owner's mark. The mark bears his own name: "on the unanswerable evidence of the paint-stain, I had discovered Myself as the Thief." He manages to see Rachel. The conversation opens with reproaches on both sides, and Rachel breaks: "You villain, I saw you take the Diamond with my own eyes!"

Franklin answers with words that hold the whole tail: "I can't explain the contradiction in what I am going to tell you. I can only speak the truth as you have spoken it." There are two truths, and they are opposites. Then he finds the exact words: "You are the victim, and I am the victim, of some monstrous delusion which has worn the mask of truth." And the most important: "You have tried by yourself. You have not tried with me to help you."

Even then the conversation breaks down. Having heard her account of the night, Franklin reproaches her — if only she had spoken then… — and a year of silence comes out in a single cry. Wen, writing of The Moon reversed, has an exact phrase: "any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing". What is held down does not vanish; it waits for an occasion.

Among The Moon's tasks Lisovskaya also names the habit of hiding feelings and taking tenderness for weakness, and an image created at the start that later collapses. The novel shows why The Moon is more dangerous than an ordinary lie. The image "Franklin the thief" was built not on gossip but on her own eyes, and that is why it lasts a whole year. A mistake taken from someone else's words is easy to check. A mistake seen with your own eyes you do not want to check: "but I saw it".

The numbers hint at how this mistake is built. The couple's main task is folded from Justice (8) of one partner and The Wheel of Fortune (10) of the other. Our reading: a verdict plus circumstances makes fog. Rachel passed an honest verdict on what she saw. She did not know the circumstances: at dinner Mr Candy, the family's medical man, had argued with Franklin about medicine and decided to teach the scoffer a lesson, and the laudanum was slipped to him in secret. In his preface Collins says he set out "to trace the influence of character on circumstances", and the couple's main task lies exactly at that seam. Character is not to blame, circumstances are not to blame; the mistake is a verdict passed alone.
For a couple with 18-18-18 the main task sounds simple: before saying "I know", say "I saw" — and ask. Not because eyes lie. Because they are looking into a mirror.

sections.h2: Ezra Jennings's black ink and red
paragraphs: The way out of the fog is found by a man nobody thinks of at first. Ezra Jennings is Mr Candy's assistant, an outsider with startling white and black hair. For years he has lived under "the cloud of a horrible accusation" that he cannot even bring himself to name; he can only assert his innocence. When the slander first struck him down, he parted with the woman he loved rather than make her share his disgrace. A man who has spent his life inside someone else's false image knows better than anyone the price of silence kept out of love.

When Mr Candy lay in a fever, Jennings took down his delirium in shorthand. Then he copied the fragments in black ink and filled the gaps between them in red, so that what was said and his interpretation stood side by side and could be checked against each other. "I have penetrated through the obstacle of the disconnected expression, to the thought which was underlying it connectedly all the time." Out of black fragments and red links a story grew. At dinner Franklin had quipped in front of everyone that "taking medicine and groping in the dark mean one and the same thing", and Mr Candy decided to give him "five-and-twenty minims of laudanum … without his knowing it" and confront him with the truth in the morning.

For a couple with three Moons this is the best working tool. The Moon writes in red ink and forgets that it is red. "He came home late" is black. "He is hiding something" is red. As long as both colours are visible to both people, any story can be checked. When red is passed off as black, a year of silence begins.

Jennings's second step is bolder. He proposes not to interrogate but to repeat the night. On 25 June 1849, almost a year after the birthday, the house is set back the way it was that night, an imitation stone goes into the cabinet drawer, and Franklin is given laudanum again. Rachel stands in her room behind a door left ajar, her light put out. Franklin gets up with a candle, mutters "How do I know? The Indians may be hidden in the house", goes to the sitting-room, opens the drawers and takes out the stone — exactly as a year before. The celebrated Cuff looked for someone to blame and was wrong about the main thing. The outsider Jennings rebuilt the circumstances and showed how it had all happened.
Wen has a short comparison of two cards: "Key 5: The Hierophant is about orthodox wisdom; Key 9 is the unorthodox solitary path to wisdom." Cuff and Jennings are those two cards in person.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the centre: a silence made of three Moons
paragraphs: At the centre of the chart every couple with the 18-18-18 tail has The Hermit (9), and he stands in the couple's values too, without exception. This is one of the strongest clues in the tail.

Lisovskaya suggests adding up repeated energies: 18 + 18 + 18 = 54, which folds to 9. The sum of the three Moons is The Hermit. By her rule, a sum that does not appear on the chart sounds in the couple only as a faint trail. Here it is no trail: it stands at the very centre.

There is a second piece of arithmetic. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is built from its ends, and between two Moons The Hermit would stand: 18 + 18 = 36 → 9. For a couple the middle is taken from the partners' middles, 5 + 13, so a third Moon appears. The silence missing from the middle of the tail has moved to the centre of the chart. In our search through all dates, the partners' personal centres in such couples are also always the same: The Chariot (7) for one, Judgement (20) for the other. Two loud cards, drive and calling, add up to silence.

For Lisovskaya the couple's centre is the atmosphere between the two, what lies inside and is not on show. With The Hermit it is a couple where each has a time and a corner of their own, where love is proved by deeds rather than words, and no step is hurried. In the minus the same Hermit paints another picture: each on their own, with difficulties piling up in silence. The scene is familiar: an evening, two people in different rooms, each "sorting it out alone" so as not to burden the other. This is exactly where the fog of the second Moon thickens.

In The Moonstone The Hermit even slips into the comedy. In every trouble old Betteredge opens Robinson Crusoe at random and reads the answer as prophecy; he has worn out six copies, and his mistress gave him a seventh. The oracle of that house is a book about a man who lived twenty-eight years on a desert island.

Waite, meanwhile, insists that The Hermit is not isolation. Reading the card through "occult isolation" he calls one of the "frivolous renderings"; for him it is "a card of attainment", a figure "holding up his beacon on an eminence". That is how Jennings leaves the novel. Before he dies he asks that not even the plainest stone mark his grave: "Let me sleep, nameless. Let me rest, unknown." The light that led the couple out of the fog was held by a man who asked for nothing in return. The values of a couple with The Hermit are his path: patient attention instead of a verdict.

After the experiment Franklin falls asleep on the sofa in that same sitting-room. Rachel asks to sit with him, watches him all night and does not set a single stitch of her needlework. By eight in the morning, Jennings writes, she is kneeling by the sofa: "She has so placed herself that when his eyes first open, they must open on her face."
In this scene the plot of the tail closes. A year earlier she saw him in a mirror, sideways, by the light of someone else's candle. Now it is face to face.

Near its end, the same hymn to love that "beareth all things" says: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:12). Paul's Greek says literally "through a mirror, in a riddle". The Russian Synodal Bible renders "in a riddle" as gadatel'no, a word from fortune-telling. The couple's three Moons fit into a single line here: the mirror, the riddle, knowledge in part. And so does the way out: not only to know the other, but to let oneself be known — "even as also I am known".

Collins built the whole novel on this principle. The plan comes from Franklin himself: each witness in turn is to write the story of the Moonstone "as far as our own personal experience extends, and no farther". No narrator knows everything. The truth appears only when the partial accounts are laid side by side. That is the form of conversation that suits a couple with three Moons: each speaks of what they saw themselves, and the story is put together by two.

Rachel and Franklin were married on 9 October 1849. In the epilogue the diamond shines again in the forehead of the Moon god, and the last narrator writes: "So the years pass, and repeat each other; so the same events revolve in the cycles of time." For a couple with the 18-18-18 tail this is not a sentence but a description of the mechanism: the same night will keep repeating until the two of them look at it together.

ul: **Two colours of ink.** Say "I saw" and "I thought" separately. Black is the fact, red is the guess, and both colours are visible to the partner.
**Don't guard with silence.** Rachel's silence was love, and it cost a year. The one who protects is not the one who kept quiet but the one who asked, in time and gently.
**Investigate together.** "You have tried by yourself. You have not tried with me" — in this couple a suspicion is taken apart at a shared table, not inside one head.

**Reconstruct, don't interrogate.** Go back to the moment where the versions parted and walk through it again: who was where, what each saw, what each thought. Interrogation looks for someone to blame; reconstruction looks for the picture.
**Keep the solitude, but don't hide in it.** The Hermit at the centre needs time alone; difficulties are not hidden there but set aside for a conversation.
**Leave the mystery room to play.** Fantasy, pet words and a shared invented world are the couple's strength. Mystery as a game — yes; mystery as a rule of conduct — no.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: Wen puts The Moon briefly: "Key 18 represents poetry and mystery." A couple with three Moons has more of that poetry than most. Lisovskaya, describing The Moon in its plus, draws a union where the partner is first of all a friend, where each understands the other from half a word, and where every year a person reveals a new side to the other. That is the strong version of 18-18-18: two people who never stop surprising each other, because they do not turn mystery into a weapon.

A strong couple with this tail keeps its door with the griffins — its shared world — and can still read the smear on it out loud. It is not afraid of silence, because The Hermit at the centre teaches them to be quiet together, not apart. And it knows the price of a reflection: a mirror honestly shows the hand, but not the thought behind it.

On the wedding day Betteredge opened Robinson Crusoe at page three hundred and eighteen and, of course, took it for a prophecy. The couple's tail prophesies nothing. It shows where to look: not into the mirror, but into the face.

sections.h2: How the 18-18-18 couple tail is calculated
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, folded down to 22. The middle of the tail is not recalculated from the couple's ends: it is the sum of the partners' middles.
An example with the dates 14.08.1975 and 04.01.1976. The first date has the personal tail 15-5-8 and centre 7, the second the tail 3-13-10 and centre 20.
What every couple with this tail has in common:

ul: **Rarity.** Roughly one couple in 1,684 (0.059%), 88th place out of 97 couple tails.

**One combination.** The tail comes only from the personal tails 15-5-8 in one partner and 3-13-10 in the other. The rarity comes from the second: in our search, since 1900 the 3-13-10 tail has fallen on only 149 birthdays, against 4,275 for 15-5-8.
**Nobody's Moon.** Neither partner has The Moon in their personal tail; the three Moons appear only in the sum.
**The Hermit.** The couple's centre is The Hermit in 100% of such couples, and the couple's values are The Hermit in 100% too.
**The middle.** It does not equal the folded sum of the ends: 18 + 18 would give 9, while the couple has 18.

paragraphs: As a personal tail the order 18-18-18 does not occur: in a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 18 an entry of 18 is impossible whatever the centre. The tail has no permutations, since all three numbers are the same; 18-9-18 is a different couple tail. In our example the whole couple chart is written with two numbers, 9 and 18, but that is rare: in our search, 0.85% of couples with this tail. Usually other arcana stand on the remaining points.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Moon.** The couple's common language is mystery. What draws them together is what cannot be seen to the bottom, and very quickly they build a world of their own: words, games and images no one else understands.

**N · Middle of the task — The Moon.** The road runs through dusk. Each notices something, guesses at something and stays silent to protect the other — and two different versions of one story live under one roof.
**D · Main task — The Moon.** To separate what was seen from what was filled in, and to check the versions together instead of passing sentence alone.

intro: At the centre of the chart every such couple has The Hermit, and The Hermit again in the couple's values: a silence in which the fog either gathers or clears. What follows is an investigation. The evidence lies in the numbers themselves, in the books of Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya, and in a novel where the key evidence of a love affair was seen in a mirror.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-18-18 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is three Moons in a couple's tail. At the entry the couple is bound by a mystery and a shared world of images; in the middle each stays silent to protect the other and keeps a private version of events; and the main task is to learn to separate what was seen from what was filled in, and to check the versions together. At the centre such couples always have The Hermit: a silence in which the fog either gathers or clears.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 18-18-18 come about?
faq.a: Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, folded down to 22. The 18-18-18 tail occurs only when one partner has the personal tail 15-5-8 and the other 3-13-10: 15 + 3, 5 + 13 and 8 + 10 give three Moons. An example is the couple 14.08.1975 and 04.01.1976.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 18 and not 9?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends but added up from the partners' middles: 5 + 13 = 18. By the personal formula 18 + 18 would fold to 9, giving a different tail, 18-9-18. The Hermit does not disappear, though: in every couple with this tail he stands at the centre of the chart.

faq.q: Does the 18-18-18 tail occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 18 an entry of 18 is impossible whatever the centre. Three Moons in a row is a tail that only a couple can have.

faq.q: Is the 18-18-18 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass sentence on the union. It shows what the two have to learn: to say "I saw" before "I know", not to guard each other with silence, and to work through misunderstandings together. In its strong version this is a couple with a rich shared imagination who understand each other from half a word.

report: Three mirrors hung in Rachel Verinder's sitting-room, and in one of them she watched the man she loved steal her diamond. This scene from Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone describes the couple tail 18-18-18 almost word for word: three Moons in a row are three mirrors in which two people see each other. The reflection was true: Franklin Blake's hand really did take the stone from the drawer. Everything else was wrong. Franklin had been secretly dosed with laudanum; that night he walked as if in a dream and remembered nothing. **A couple with this tail knows each other by reflection: the fact is seen precisely, the meaning is not.**

report.h3: The door that remembered the night

unit.meaning: You know each other by reflection, and the fog clears when you work things out together, not each alone.
